projects.name: Vault — zero-knowledge password manager
projects.summary: A password manager you run on your own server. Everything is encrypted in the browser; the server stores ciphertext it holds no key for. Live on an always-free OCI instance for $0 a month.
highlights: AES-256-GCM in the browser; the master password is never sent — the server gets a separate HKDF branch, stored only as an scrypt verifier
Names, websites, notes, folders and tags are encrypted too, so a database dump doesn't even reveal which sites you use
Organizations, groups and collections, each with its own key, sealed to members confirmed by fingerprint
Pull-based releases: the host verifies a SHA-256 manifest, health-checks the new build and rolls back on failure; SSH stays closed
350 unit and 20 browser tests in CI; encrypted backups restore onto SQLite or PostgreSQL
projects.body:
## What it is

Vault is a zero-knowledge password manager. The master password never leaves the browser; keys are derived there, every field is encrypted there, and the server only ever sees ciphertext. A complete compromise of the server should yield nothing more.

![The Vault web app: folders and types, items, and a login with a live one-time code](/uploads/proj-vault-vault.webp)

## What it does

- **Fifteen item types** — logins, notes, cards, identities, bank accounts, passports, SSH keys, API credentials, Wi-Fi and more — with custom fields, folders four levels deep and live one-time codes.
- **Password health** — weak, reused, year-old and `http://`-only passwords, scored out of 100 with advice on each item, computed in the browser.
- **History you can restore** — every edit keeps the previous version, encrypted like the item.
- **Import from nine formats** — Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Bitwarden, 1Password, LastPass, KeePass, Zoho Vault and more, previewed before anything is saved.
- **A browser extension** for Chrome and Firefox that fills only where the site truly matches, so a look-alike page gets nothing.

![Password health: a score with advice on what to fix](/uploads/proj-vault-health.webp)

## Built for teams too

Organizations, groups and collections, each with its own key, sealed to every member you confirm by fingerprint. Permissions, policies, an audit log, key rotation and emergency access — plus an admin console and a built-in service desk for access requests and support tickets. None of it can read a vault.

![Members of an organization, confirmed by fingerprint](/uploads/proj-vault-organizations.webp)

## Runs on your own server

One command on a Linux machine with Docker asks for the address, generates the secrets, starts Vault and prints the link that creates the owner account. Two editions from one codebase: **Personal** (one account, SQLite) and **Business** (people, groups and policies, PostgreSQL).

![The public website](/uploads/proj-vault-website.webp)

pages.title: Security design
pages.summary: The key hierarchy, where trust ends, and the one risk accepted knowingly.
pages.body:
## Where trust ends

Everything below the browser is assumed hostile. That assumption drives three choices that would otherwise look excessive:

- **The master password is never transmitted.** The server receives an *Auth Key*, a separate HKDF branch of the Master Key, and stores only an scrypt verifier of it.
- **All entry content is encrypted client-side**, including names, tags and folder names. The server cannot read, search or index any of it.
- **Email addresses are stored as HMAC digests** under a pepper kept outside the database, so a dump does not identify account holders.

## Key hierarchy

```
Master password + per-user salt
        │ PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 rounds
        ▼
   Master Key ──┬── HKDF "vault.kek.v1"  ──► KEK ──► wraps the Vault Key
                └── HKDF "vault.auth.v1" ──► Auth Key ──► server (scrypt verifier)

   Vault Key (random, generated once)
        ├── wrapped by the KEK            (master password)
        ├── wrapped by the Recovery KEK   (recovery key)
        └── encrypts every field, AES-256-GCM, fresh 96-bit IV
```

Because a random Vault Key encrypts everything and the master password only wraps it, **changing the password is a single write**: nothing is re-encrypted and history survives. A recovery key, shown once at sign-up, is the only way back from a forgotten password — there is no reset, because the server cannot perform one.

Each account also has an ECDH P-256 identity key pair, which is how a collection key reaches a colleague without the server learning it.

![Every previous version, encrypted like the item](/uploads/proj-vault-history.webp)

## The risk accepted on purpose

The hostname is a free dynamic-DNS name, and it is the whole user-facing trust path: whoever controls that name could serve their own JavaScript, which would see the master password. Unlike a server compromise, that is not bounded by the key hierarchy. It is written down in the threat model and accepted knowingly for a $0 deployment, rather than hidden.

pages.title: Shipping and running it
pages.summary: Pull-based releases with automatic rollback, monitoring, backups and a service desk — on one always-free instance.
pages.body:
## Releases the host pulls

Code reaches the server by the server pulling it. Every merge to `main` runs CI (crypto, core, API, web, site, end-to-end, audit) and GitHub Actions uploads a tarball with a SHA-256 manifest to a releases bucket, using a cloud user that can write that bucket and nothing else.

On the host, a timer checks every five minutes, verifies the hash and the manifest, validates the Caddyfile, installs, checks the service through Caddy, and **reinstalls the previous release if anything fails**. Nothing inbound is involved; SSH stays closed.

```
pull request ──CI──▶ merge to main ──▶ releases bucket (tarball + SHA-256 manifest)
                                              │ every 5 min
                                              ▼
                              host: verify → install → health check
                                              │ fails
                                              ▼
                                   reinstall the previous release
```

## One always-free instance

Caddy terminates TLS and serves the public website at `/`, the vault client at `/app/` and the Node API at `/api/` (localhost only). A probe reports metrics every five minutes, and cloud monitoring alarms reach me by email and push.

## Backups that restore anywhere

One encrypted file holds everything and restores onto SQLite or PostgreSQL, from disk or any S3-compatible store — tested in CI on every change.

## Support built in

A service desk handles access requests, lost authenticators and support tickets, without any of it being able to read a vault.

![A service desk ticket](/uploads/proj-vault-desk-ticket.webp)

projects.name: Pahredar — self-hosted security intelligence
projects.summary: A self-hosted CVE intelligence platform: a local copy of every published CVE, enriched with exploitation, exploit and detection data from free public sources, kept current hourly, plus a security news feed and an endpoint scanner.
highlights: The full CVE corpus (430k+ records) from the official CVE List, synced hourly and enriched with NVD, CISA KEV, EPSS, Exploit-DB, Metasploit and Nuclei data
Detection guidance per CVE: version checks, Nuclei, Nmap and Metasploit checks, Suricata and Sigma rules, ATT&CK and CAPEC context
Security news from 67 vendor, CERT, research and news sources, ranked by exploited and widely covered CVEs
A modular monolith in Go: three services (intelligence, news, scanner) over a shared core, one binary, Postgres full-text search
Idempotent, cursor-based sync with per-source locks, isolated failures and backoff; every run is logged
projects.body:
## Why I built it

Tracking vulnerabilities properly means stitching together a dozen free sources: the CVE List, NVD, CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, EPSS, exploit databases, detection rules and vendor advisories. Pahredar (Hindi for *watchman*) keeps all of it in one local database and answers the questions that matter for a CVE: how bad is it, is it being exploited, is there a public exploit, what does it affect, and how do I detect and fix it.

![The dashboard: critical CVEs this week, publish volume by severity, trending in the news](/uploads/proj-pahredar-dash.webp)

## Every CVE, enriched

- **The full corpus** from the official CVE List, current within the hour, with full-text search and filters by severity, KEV, exploit availability, vendor, product, CWE, dates and EPSS.
- **Exploitation evidence** beyond CISA KEV: ENISA EUVD and VulnCheck KEV, plus likely-exploited CVEs not yet in KEV and the biggest EPSS increases.
- **Detection and response** on each CVE: version-check commands, Nuclei / Nmap / Metasploit checks, Suricata and Sigma rules, ATT&CK mappings, fixed versions, distro status and vendor advisories.

![A CVE in detail: Log4Shell with its signals, exploitation and tabs for detection, ATT&CK and remediation](/uploads/proj-pahredar-cve.webp)

![The CVE explorer: 430k+ CVEs with query syntax and filters](/uploads/proj-pahredar-search.webp)

## Security news, ranked

Sixty-seven vendor, national CERT, research, mailing-list and news sources are synced hourly into a security brief, ranked by exploited and widely covered CVEs, with Google News, Hacker News and Bluesky coverage per CVE.

![The security brief](/uploads/proj-pahredar-news.webp)

## Vendors and products

Vendor and product pages show the severity mix and CVEs per year, so it's easy to see who is shipping the most critical bugs.

![Apache Software Foundation: severity mix and CVEs per year](/uploads/proj-pahredar-vendor.webp)

pages.title: Under the hood
pages.summary: A modular monolith in Go over Postgres, and a sync engine that keeps 430k+ records current without ever clobbering data.
pages.body:
## One binary, three services

```
 external sources: cvelistV5 · NVD · CISA KEV · EPSS · Exploit-DB · Metasploit · Nuclei · feeds
                               │ scheduled HTTPS pulls
 ┌─────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
 │ backend (Go, single binary)                                │
 │   intelligence · news · endpoint scanner   (services)      │
 │   store · config · scheduler · job queue · HTTP  (core)    │
 └───────────────▲─────────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                 │ JSON                         │ SQL (pgx)
      React + Vite frontend               Postgres: source of truth
      (nginx, proxies /api)               + full-text search
```

Pahredar is a **modular monolith**: each product service owns its domain over a shared core. One deployable, because a single operator and $0 hosting rule out microservices, but clear seams so services grow independently. Cross-service reads go through named interfaces — the scanner asks intelligence "which CVEs affect this technology?" without touching its internals.

## A sync engine you can trust

- **Idempotent:** every job is an upsert, so re-running a job or replaying a window is safe.
- **Cursor-based:** incremental jobs only advance their cursor after a successful commit.
- **Never concurrent with itself:** a Postgres advisory lock guards each source.
- **Failures are isolated:** a failing source doesn't block the others; it is retried with exponential backoff.
- **Bulk loads use `COPY`** into a staging table, then one `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`.
- **No clobbering:** CVE writes are serialised and every writer derives the row from both the CVE List and NVD records, so neither job can overwrite the other's contribution with stale data.

The first start streams the ~615 MB CVE List archive without writing it all to disk, pulls NVD four pages at a time inside its rate limit, and the database ends up around 4.5 GB.

![Data sync: every source, its last success and cursor, with a manual run button](/uploads/proj-pahredar-sync.webp)

## Built with

Go (standard library HTTP, pgx, goose migrations embedded in the binary), Postgres 17 with `tsvector` full-text search and `pg_trgm`, React + Vite + TypeScript with TanStack Query, Tailwind and Recharts, all run with Docker Compose.

projects.name: Multi-cloud Infrastructure as Code
projects.summary: Terraform monorepo with isolated state per provider, a single Makefile entry point and remote state in OCI Object Storage.
highlights: One state file per provider, so any provider can be planned, applied or destroyed on its own.
Placed workloads across five providers' free tiers after verifying limits in provider docs; runs at $0/month.
projects.body:
## Why I rebuilt it

My earlier setup kept every provider in one Terraform state, and the bucket holding that state was created by the same Terraform. Destroying one thing meant destroying the backend that held it, halfway through a run.

## What I built

One repository and one command interface, but **one state file per provider**: Oracle Cloud, AWS, Cloudflare and GitHub. Any provider can be planned, applied or destroyed on its own without touching the others.

![make help: one Makefile drives every stack](/uploads/proj-infra-help.webp)

- **`make bootstrap` is a script, not Terraform.** Terraform cannot create the bucket that holds its own state, so one small manual step removes that cycle for good.
- **`make verify`** checks every provider credential in a couple of seconds, because an expired token otherwise shows up as a confusing Terraform error.
- **`make retry`** keeps applying a stack until free-tier capacity frees up, and `make retry-status` shows how far it got.
- **No secrets in the repository.** Each provider authenticates the way its own tooling expects, and `terraform.tfvars` is never committed; examples carry the shape, not the values.

## Status

The scaffolding is complete and every stack initialises. Resources are being written stack by stack; the rules below keep it from drifting into the old coupling.

pages.title: The rules that keep it clean
pages.summary: Four rules that stop one provider's change from breaking another, or a free estate from starting to cost money.
pages.body:
![The repository layout](/uploads/proj-infra-tree.webp)

## Each stack owns its own state

Never reference one stack's resources from another through remote state. If two stacks need the same value, it is passed as a variable. Cross-stack references would recreate exactly the coupling this layout exists to avoid.

## `terraform.tfvars` is never committed

Copy `terraform.tfvars.example` and fill it in. Credentials come from each provider's own config (`~/.oci/config`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `gh auth`), so nothing secret ever lands in git.

## Free-tier constraints are load-bearing

Several resources have settings that must not drift: capacity modes, absent VPC attachments, specific billing modes. Each one is commented where it applies, with the reason. Changing one of them is how a free estate starts costing money.

## Nothing here creates content

This repository manages infrastructure and settings only. Application code and site content live in their own repositories, so destroying a stack never destroys work.

projects.name: Dohra — local class recorder
projects.summary: Open-source Chromium extension that records a class playing in a browser tab and transcribes it on your own computer — no bot joins the meeting and nothing is uploaded.
highlights: Go companion running whisper.cpp for live local transcription, including Hinglish in Roman script.
Signed releases with one-click self-update, subtitles, search across transcripts and bookmarks.
projects.body:
*Dohra* comes from the Hindi *dohrana*, "to revise". Live classes move faster than anyone can take notes; Dohra keeps the whole class so you can go back to it.

## What it does

Dohra records any online class or meeting in Chrome, Edge or Brave, on your own computer, with a searchable Hinglish transcript that knows who said what.

![Recording from the toolbar popup](/uploads/proj-dohra-popup.webp)

- **Private by design.** Recordings and transcripts are written to your own disk. No server, no account, nothing uploaded.
- **No bot in the meeting.** It records what the browser already plays, so nobody sees an extra attendee. Works on Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Zoom's web client, YouTube Live or a course's own player.
- **Hinglish transcripts.** Hindi in Roman script ("theek hai"), English as English, made on your computer while the class runs.
- **Bookmarks and search.** Press <kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd> during class to mark a moment; one search box finds a word in any recording and plays from that line.

![A recording with its transcript and bookmarks](/uploads/proj-dohra-session.webp)

## Shipping it properly

Dohra is MIT licensed and released on GitHub. Every download is checked against a pinned SHA-256, updates must be signed, and Settings can check for and install a new version in one click.

pages.title: How it works
pages.summary: A Manifest V3 extension plus an optional Go companion that runs whisper.cpp locally. No server anywhere.
pages.body:
Dohra is a Manifest V3 extension for Chromium browsers, plus an optional local companion program written in Go that transcribes with whisper.cpp.

```
popup ─▶ background (service worker) ─▶ offscreen document (the recorder)
                                              │ chunks
                                              ▼
                                   storage worker ─▶ OPFS ─▶ Downloads/Dohra/

offscreen ─16 kHz PCM─▶ background ══native messaging══▶ dohra-companion (Go) ─▶ whisper-cli
```

## Recording

The background service worker gets a tab capture stream and hands it to an offscreen document, which records in chunks. A dedicated storage worker does all file I/O into the browser's private file system (OPFS), then the finished file is copied to `Downloads/Dohra/`. Interrupted recordings are recovered on the next start.

## Transcription

Speech recognition runs outside the browser: the extension sends 16 kHz audio over native messaging to the companion, which runs whisper.cpp chunk by chunk and streams lines back. The transcript is saved next to the recording and survives crashes and closed browsers.

## Who said what

In Google Meet and Microsoft Teams, each line is labelled with the speaker's name, taken from the meeting's own active-speaker indicator.

![Speaker names in the transcript](/uploads/proj-dohra-speakers.webp)

## Search everything

The library searches every recording's title and transcript, and a result opens the recording at that line.

![Searching across recordings](/uploads/proj-dohra-search.webp)

projects.name: DevOps Assessment Platform
projects.summary: Online exam platform with live invigilation, containerised with Docker Compose; hosted on EC2 for a campus hiring drive at JBIT.
highlights: Live invigilation with camera and screen capture.
Fully containerised with Docker Compose for one-command deployment.
projects.body:
An internal hiring assessment platform: multiple-choice and short-answer questions, hands-on Linux tasks in a real browser terminal, and programming questions whose code actually runs against test cases, all scored automatically with a human override where it matters. Every component is free and open source.

## For administrators

Build a reusable question bank across the DevOps syllabus, compose exams from it with sections and scheduling, assign candidates, watch the exam live, review every answer, override any score with a recorded reason, and export results.

![The question bank](/uploads/proj-assessment-questions.webp)

## For candidates

No account to create: they register with the exam code they were sent, sign in with email, exam code and password, acknowledge the rules, and start. Coding questions get their own workspace, with the problem on the left and an editor and console on the right, in Python, JavaScript, Java or Bash.

## Question types

| Type | How it is scored |
|---|---|
| MCQ / MSQ | One correct option, or set comparison with partial credit |
| Short answer | Accepted answers as plain text, a regex or a number within a tolerance |
| Practical | A per-candidate flag planted in an isolated Linux container |
| Programming | The same test cases judge every language |

![A question with its answer key](/uploads/proj-assessment-question.webp)

pages.title: Security model
pages.summary: How an exam stays fair when candidates run real commands and real code.
pages.body:
## The clock belongs to the server

`expires_at` is written once when an attempt starts. Refreshing, reopening in another browser or clearing storage changes nothing, and a sweeper closes and grades attempts whose time has run out.

## Per-candidate flags

A practical answer is an HMAC of the attempt and question, so two candidates solving the same task submit different strings. A leaked flag scores nothing and shows whose attempt it came from. The flag is never stored and never sent to the browser.

## Candidate code never runs on the application server

The API has no Docker access at all. It writes a job row; a separate worker owns the Docker socket and runs the code in a throwaway container with no network, a read-only root filesystem, an unprivileged user, every capability dropped, and memory, CPU, PID and wall-clock limits.

## Terminals are proxied, not exposed

A lab container publishes no host port. The only way in is an authenticated WebSocket through the API, which checks that the attempt belongs to the person asking and is still running.

## Leaving the exam blanks it

Switching tab, losing focus or leaving fullscreen covers the paper with a lockout, while the clock keeps running underneath. One alt-tab fires two browser events milliseconds apart, so they are de-duplicated, and developer-tool shortcuts are swallowed with a quiet note.

projects.name: This portfolio
projects.summary: A static, multi-theme portfolio with a points game, a Git-based admin panel and a learning site — built on Astro and served by Caddy from an always-free OCI VM.
highlights: One content model rendered by three entirely different themes.
Content edited in an admin panel; every save is a Git commit that CI builds and deploys.
projects.body:
The site you are on. One set of content, three entirely different themes, a game layered on top, and an admin panel, served for $0 a month.

## Three themes, one content model

Every page is a list of blocks (banner, cards, projects, experience…), and each theme renders each block its own way. **Studio** is clean and editorial; **Terminal** is a shell with a virtual filesystem and five CTF flags to find; **Quest** is a pixel adventure.

![Terminal: a shell you can actually type into](/uploads/proj-portfolio-terminal.webp)

![Quest: the same content as a pixel adventure](/uploads/proj-portfolio-quest.webp)

## A game you play by reading

Visiting pages, opening projects, running terminal commands and capturing flags earn XP and coins. Coins buy the Terminal and Quest themes and extra palettes. Guests play in the browser; signing in with Google or GitHub saves progress. A live count shows who else is here, with anonymous cursors on the same page.

## Edited like a real product

A custom admin panel edits pages, projects, experience, posts, courses and media. Every save is a Git commit, so CI tests and deploys it, and any change can be reviewed or reverted.

pages.title: How it's built
pages.summary: Astro static sites, a small Go API with SQLite, Caddy on an always-free VM, and CI that tests everything before it deploys.
pages.body:
## The stack

- **Astro** builds the portfolio and the learn site as static HTML, from one `content/` folder.
- **A Go API** with SQLite handles sign-in (OAuth / OpenID Connect), saved progress, the coin shop, live presence over WebSockets and the admin endpoints.
- **Caddy** serves everything from one always-free Oracle Cloud VM with automatic HTTPS.
- **GitHub Actions** runs unit tests, Go tests and a browser test suite against the real API binary, then deploys over SSH with a key restricted to rsync.

## Clean URLs with themes

URLs never contain the theme. Each theme is built separately, the visitor's choice lives in a cookie, and Caddy serves the matching build for the same path.

## Trusting points from a browser

Clients can send anything, so the API only accepts events listed in a game catalog generated from the content at build time. Points come from the catalog, never from the browser, and the site and API are built from the same commit so they always agree.

## Content as code

The admin panel commits through the GitHub API. An invalid edit fails the build instead of breaking the live site, and every change is versioned.
